---
title: "Aliases: keeping old URLs working"
---

## Overview

When a page moves or gets renamed, every link, bookmark and search
result pointing at its old URL breaks. The `aliases:` key keeps those
URLs working: list the old paths in the page's front matter, and
Quarto writes a small redirect at each one.

```yaml
---
title: Deploying content
aliases:
  - /old-deploy-guide.html
  - /cookbook/deploying/
---
```

Rendering this site produces the page itself plus two extra files —
`_site/old-deploy-guide.html` and `_site/cookbook/deploying/index.html`
— each a redirect to the real page.

Aliases only take effect in **website** projects. In any other project
type Quarto warns that the key has no effect rather than ignoring it.

## Writing an alias

An alias is a URL path, not a source path. It names where the page
*used to be* in the built site.

**A leading `/` is relative to the site root.** This is almost always
what you want, and it means the same thing no matter where the page
declaring it lives:

```yaml
aliases:
  - /guides/deploy.html
```

**Anything else is relative to the page's own location** in the output.
A page that renders to `_site/current/index.html` writing:

```yaml
aliases:
  - ../previous/index.html
```

gets a redirect at `_site/previous/index.html`.

### Paths that name a directory

An alias that ends in `/`, or that has no file extension, names a
directory — Quarto adds `index.html`:

| Alias            | Redirect written at        |
| ---------------- | -------------------------- |
| `/deploy/`       | `_site/deploy/index.html`   |
| `/deploy`        | `_site/deploy/index.html`   |
| `/deploy.html`   | `_site/deploy.html`         |

The first two are equivalent. Use the third form only when the old URL
really did end in `.html`.

## Fragments

An alias may carry a `#fragment`, which is useful when one old page was
split into several new ones. Each fragment can lead somewhere different:

```yaml
# building.qmd
aliases:
  - /hub/            # the bare URL lands here
  - /hub/#image

# deploying.qmd
aliases:
  - /hub/#deploy     # a different page
```

Both pages contribute to a single redirect at `_site/hub/index.html`.
A visitor arriving at `/hub/#deploy` reaches *Deploying*; one arriving
at `/hub/#image`, or at plain `/hub/`, reaches *Building*.

When you use fragments this way, **one page must claim the bare URL**
(the `/hub/` entry above). Without it, a visitor who arrives with no
fragment has nowhere defined to go, and Quarto reports an error rather
than guessing.

## Drafts

A page marked `draft: true` writes no redirects. A live URL pointing at
an unfinished page would reveal its existence, which defeats the point
of marking it a draft.

## When aliases conflict

Two aliases cannot produce the same file, and an alias cannot land on a
page your project renders. Quarto treats each of these as an error and
stops the render, reporting **every** conflict it found rather than one
at a time:

- [`Q-5-23`](../../errors/project/Q-5-23.qmd) — the redirect would
  overwrite a real page.
- [`Q-5-24`](../../errors/project/Q-5-24.qmd) — two pages claim the
  same alias, or no page claims a shared alias's bare URL.
- [`Q-5-25`](../../errors/project/Q-5-25.qmd) — two paths differ only
  in capitalization.
- [`Q-5-26`](../../errors/project/Q-5-26.qmd) — the alias climbs above
  the output directory.

Stopping is deliberate. The alternative — a site that builds while a
redirect is silently missing or silently points at the wrong page — is
much harder to notice: the build log looks clean and the old links keep
failing with nothing to explain why.

## Differences from Quarto 1

If you are porting a site, three behaviours changed.

**Conflicts are errors.** Quarto 1 warns and skips when a redirect
would overwrite a page, and says nothing at all when two pages claim
the same alias — the last one processed silently wins. Quarto 2 stops
and names both pages.

**Capitalization counts, on every platform.** Quarto 1 compares paths
exactly, so `/Deploy/` and `/deploy/` look distinct to it. On macOS and
Windows they are the same file, and one silently overwrites the other —
which, when the loser is a real page, replaces that page with a
redirect pointing at itself. Quarto 2 rejects such a pair even on
Linux, so a site built in CI cannot break when served elsewhere.

**The redirect works without JavaScript.** Quarto 1's redirect runs a
script and does nothing else; a reader without JavaScript sees a blank
page, and a crawler has to infer what happened. Quarto 2 adds a
`<noscript>` fallback, a `rel="canonical"` link naming the destination,
and a visible link as a last resort. The generated file therefore
differs from Quarto 1's byte for byte — expected, and not a sign that
something went wrong with your port.
